name: Zheng He
info: Zheng He, born Ma He, was a Chinese admiral and diplomat of the early Ming dynasty, a eunuch in the service of the Yongle Emperor, who commanded seven treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433.

facts.born: 1371, as Ma He, in Kunyang, Kunming, Yunnan; of a Muslim (Hui) family descended from Sayyid Ajjal Shams al-Din Omar, governor of Yunnan under the Yuan
facts.died: 1433, probably during or shortly after his seventh voyage, perhaps at Calicut, and buried at sea; or, by another theory, at Nanjing in 1435
facts.role: Eunuch servant and commander of Zhu Di, Prince of Yan; Grand Director of the Directorate of Palace Servants from 1402; admiral and Chief Envoy of the treasure fleet from 1405 to 1433; defender of Nanjing from 1425
facts.known: the seven treasure voyages of 1405-1433; the Jingnan campaign; bringing envoys of more than thirty states to the Ming court; the giraffe taken as a qilin; the Mao Kun map; veneration among the Chinese of Southeast Asia

t: Captured as a boy in the Ming conquest of Yunnan and castrated, Ma He rose in the household of Zhu Di and helped him seize the throne as the Yongle Emperor in 1402.
As admiral he led seven voyages from 1405 to 1433 that reached Southeast Asia, India, Arabia and the Swahili coast, mixing trade and gifts with displays and use of military force.
The voyages ended under later emperors and officials played them down for centuries, until Liang Qichao's biography of 1904 made Zheng He widely known.
dyk: A giraffe Zheng He brought back from Malindi was taken in China to be a qilin, a sign of the Mandate of Heaven upon the emperor's rule.
ev: Ma He is taken prisoner by Ming armies in Yunnan, later castrated and placed in the service of the Prince of Yan
In the Jingnan campaign he defends Beiping's city reservoir against imperial armies
Zhu Di takes Nanjing and becomes the Yongle Emperor, making Ma He Grand Director
The emperor confers on him the surname Zheng
The first treasure voyage sails with 317 ships and almost 28,000 crewmen
The Yongle Emperor dies and the Hongxi Emperor halts further voyages
He completes the rebuilding of the Great Bao'en Temple at Nanjing and sets out on the seventh voyage
He probably dies during or shortly after the last voyage and is buried at sea

sections.early:
Zheng He was born Ma He in 1371 to a Muslim (Hui) family of Kunyang, Kunming, in Yunnan, which was then ruled by the Principality of Liang, loyal to the Northern Yuan dynasty. He had an older brother and four sisters. He was a great-great-great-grandson of Sayyid Ajjal Shams al-Din Omar, who served in the administration of the Mongol Empire and governed Yunnan in the early Yuan dynasty. His grandfather and his father, who bore the sinicised surname Ma, both carried the title hajji, which suggests they had made the pilgrimage to Mecca.

In the early 1380s a Ming army conquered Yunnan from the Mongol prince Basalawarmi. Ma He's father died in the fighting, at 39 according to Dreyer and at 37 according to Levathes; it is unclear whether he was helping the Mongol army or caught in the battle. The boy was taken prisoner in 1381 after answering General Fu Youde defiantly that the Mongol pretender had jumped into a lake. He was castrated between the ages of 10 and 14 and sent to serve, enslaved as a eunuch, in the household of Zhu Di, the Prince of Yan, eleven years his senior, who governed Beiping near the Mongol frontier. Later, as admiral, he had an epitaph engraved for his father in 1405.
sections.rise:
At Beiping Ma He received an education he would not have had in Nanjing, where the Hongwu Emperor distrusted eunuchs and preferred them illiterate. He spent his early years as a soldier on the northern frontier, took part in Zhu Di's campaigns against the Mongols and accompanied the prince on his first expedition in 1390, when the Mongol commander Naghachu surrendered. In the prince's household he was known as Sanbao, after the Three Jewels of Buddhism, and he became a trusted adviser. He was recorded as seven chi tall, with glaring eyes and a voice as loud as a bell, and as skilled in war.

After the Hongwu Emperor died in 1398, his grandson the Jianwen Emperor began "reducing the feudatories", stripping the princes of power. Zhu Di rebelled in August 1399, opening the Jingnan campaign. That year Ma He defended Beiping's reservoir, Zhenglunba, against the imperial armies, and in 1402 he was one of the commanders in the campaign that took Nanjing on 13 July. Zhu Di became the Yongle Emperor, the Jianwen Emperor having apparently died, and promoted Ma He to Grand Director of the Directorate of Palace Servants. In 1404 the emperor conferred on him the surname Zheng in recognition of his service at the reservoir and in the campaign for the capital.
sections.deeds:
Between 1405 and 1433 the Ming government sponsored seven naval expeditions, all under Zheng He as admiral and Chief Envoy, with Wang Jinghong as second in command. The Yongle Emperor, disregarding his father's wishes, meant them to establish a Chinese presence and imperial control over the Indian Ocean trade, impress foreign peoples and extend the tributary system; passages in the History of Ming suggest the first voyages also sought the escaped Jianwen Emperor. The first fleet left on 11 July 1405 with 317 ships and almost 28,000 crewmen, and so many interpreters were needed that a foreign language institute was founded at Nanjing.

The fleets visited Brunei, Java, Siam, India, the Horn of Africa and Arabia, along routes long used for trade. Zheng He gave gold, silver, porcelain and silk and brought back ostriches, zebras, camels and ivory from the Swahili coast and a giraffe from Malindi. From his fourth voyage he brought envoys from 30 states to the Ming court. The translator Ma Huan recorded the customs of the ports in 1416. On his travels he built mosques, spread the worship of the sea goddess Mazu, or Tianfei, and visited Muslim shrines in Fujian; the Galle Trilingual Inscription in Chinese, Tamil and Persian records the fleet's gifts to a temple in Sri Lanka. In 1424 he conferred a seal of office on Shi Jisun at Palembang.
sections.opponents:
The fleets carried troops and used force. A contemporary reported that Zheng He "walked like a tiger" and did not shrink from violence when he thought it necessary to impress foreign peoples with China's might. He suppressed pirates, defeating Chen Zuyi and sending him to China for execution, waged a land war against the Kingdom of Kotte on Ceylon, whose king Vira Alakeshwara came to China as a captive, and made displays of force when local officials threatened the fleet in Arabia and East Africa. Tansen Sen has emphasised the new militaristic presence the Ming navy brought to the Indian Ocean.

At court the voyages had opponents. They went against the Huang Ming Zuxun, the dynastic founder's injunctions, which asked that far-off countries be spared the cost of tribute, and against longstanding Confucian principles; they represented a triumph of the eunuch faction over the scholar-bureaucrats. In 1426 the Xuande Emperor had Zheng He reprimanded for prompting an official to charge the court for temple building in Nanjing, though he later came to trust him. Claims about the size of his ships have their own critics: Edward L. Dreyer calls Luo Maodeng's 1597 novel, the source of the largest figures, unsuitable as evidence, and excavation of the Treasure Shipyard in 2003-2004 suggested ships of no more than 75 metres.
sections.last:
When Zheng He returned from Palembang in 1424 he found that the Yongle Emperor had died. The Hongxi Emperor ended further voyages on 7 September 1424 and on 24 February 1425 appointed him defender of Nanjing, keeping the treasure fleet under his command for the city's defence. In 1428 the Xuande Emperor put him in charge of rebuilding the Great Bao'en Temple at Nanjing, which he completed in 1431. Before the last voyage he and his colleagues rebuilt the Tianfei Palace at Changle in Fujian and raised a stele recording their earlier voyages.

In 1430 the Xuande Emperor appointed him to command a seventh and final expedition to the Western Ocean, and in 1431 he received the title Sanbao Taijian. He apparently never made the pilgrimage to Mecca himself, but sent sailors there on this voyage. One theory holds that he died in 1433 during the voyage, probably at Calicut, or shortly after it; another that he went on serving as defender of Nanjing and died in 1435. His body was buried at sea off the Malabar Coast, and the tomb built for him on Cattle Head Hill at Nanjing is a cenotaph believed to hold his clothes and headgear; it was rebuilt in the Muslim style in 1985.
sections.legacy:
After his death and his faction's fall, his successors played him down in official accounts. The annals of the Yongle and Xuande Emperors were incomplete and even erroneous, which some have seen as a conspiracy and others as records dispersed among departments and an embarrassment to the dynasty. State naval efforts declined as funds went to wars against the Mongols and, after the disaster at Tumu in 1449, to the Great Wall, and neglect of the navy left the coast open to the wokou in the 16th century. Missions from Southeast Asia, however, continued for decades.

Among the Chinese of Southeast Asia Zheng He became a figure of folk veneration, with Sam Po temples in Jakarta, Cirebon, Surabaya and Semarang; in 1961 the Indonesian scholar Hamka credited him with an important role in the development of Islam in Indonesia. Liang Qichao's biography of 1904 made him widely known. In the 1950s John Fairbank and Joseph Needham presented the end of the voyages as China turning away from the sea; modern historians note that Chinese maritime trade continued, and Jack Goldstone argues the voyages ended for practical reasons. Richard von Glahn holds that "Zheng He reshaped Asia". In China 11 July, the day the first voyage sailed, is Maritime Day.

summary: Zheng He, a Muslim from Yunnan captured and castrated as a boy, became the Yongle Emperor's trusted eunuch commander and led seven Ming treasure voyages across the Indian Ocean from 1405 to 1433, combining trade, diplomacy and force. Neglected by later Ming officials, he is now remembered across China and Southeast Asia.

notes: The article dates the Ming conquest of Yunnan to autumn 1382 but his father's death and Ma He's capture to 1381; kept the capture at 1381 as the article states it, and wrote 'the early 1380s' for the conquest.
Death: 1433 or 1435; end set to 1433 with endCirca.
The article gives no figures for those killed in the Kotte war or the pirate battle.
The ship-size debate (Luo Maodeng's 127 m treasure ships vs. 60-75 m estimates) is summarised in 'opponents' only briefly.
